info.description:
Message store + routing core: mailbox Durable Objects, R2 blobs, D1 directory. Every route requires a bearer credential (401 unauthorized without one) except two: GET /api/v1/health, and GET /api/v1/pim/feeds/{token}, where the calendar-feed token in the path IS the credential. Mailbox-scoped app passwords are refused on directory routes with 403 insufficient_scope. Errors always answer { error: "snake_case_code", ... } — schema failures as { error: "validation_failed", issues }.

A caller holding a mailbox app password may write `me` wherever a {mailboxId} PATH segment appears — /api/v1/mailboxes/me/messages and the rest of the subtree — and the request is served as though it had named that credential's own mailbox id. It is a path convenience only: a mailboxId inside a request BODY always names a resource explicitly. Any other principal gets 404, since `me` has no referent for an account or system key.

post.description:
**The SMTP-shaped route: for submission agents, not applications.** One recipient per call — you fan out and collect a verdict per RCPT, mirroring an SMTP transaction. Application code almost always wants `POST /mailboxes/{mailboxId}/send`, which takes JSON, builds the MIME, and returns every recipient's result from one call.

**Response codes are durable guarantees.** `200 delivered` comes only after the full two-phase commit; `202 queued` only once the blob is durably staged and a queue job exists. For an MTA the mapping is `4xx` = permanent failure (bounce), `5xx` = retry with the same `X-Delivery-Id` — the retry converges, because everything in the delivery path is idempotent.

Every RFC 5322 `From:` address must ladder-resolve to the sending mailbox on a domain that may send (`invalid_from` / `from_not_owned` / `from_sending_disabled`), which is what keeps the outbound DKIM signature DMARC-aligned.

get.description:
Two representations of the same resource. Without an `Accept: application/json` header you get the stored bytes verbatim — what a DAV client needs. With it you get a JSContact Card (RFC 9553), which is what a browser client wants: no vCard parser in the page, and unmapped properties preserved through a read-modify-write by the escape hatches.

**The ETag is the hash of the WIRE bytes in both representations** — it validates the resource, not the encoding, so an `If-Match` taken from a JSON read is valid on a raw write and vice versa.

`data` is null when the stored body has no JSON mapping — a body that does not parse — and `content` carries the wire text in that case. `writable` is false when the object converts to JSON but could not be converted back — it is display-only.

post.description:
The one call behind a mail client's Accept / Tentative / Decline buttons. Name the invitation — either `messageId` (+ the `section` from `…/messages/{id}/invitation`, or omit it and let the server pick the scheduling part) or the raw `ics` inline — and give a PARTSTAT; it files an attendee copy into the default calendar if the event is not already stored, then records the reply and tells the organizer — patching their copy in place when they are local, mailing them a `METHOD:REPLY` when they are not.

Prefer `messageId`: the bytes are already here, so the inline form makes a client fetch the part, decode its charset, and post it straight back.

**Why this exists rather than PUT-then-respond.** Writing the invitation yourself and then replying is the natural client shape and is unsafe: a PUT whose ORGANIZER is the writing mailbox schedules iTIP, so an ICS that names *you* as organizer would turn one click on unsolicited mail into invitations sent as you, to addresses the sender chose. This endpoint refuses exactly that — the caller must be an ATTENDEE and must not be the ORGANIZER — and the filing it performs is an attendee copy, which never schedules.

**The loop.** Call once with no `since` to get a starting `newState`; do your full listing; then poll with `since=<newState>`, or better, subscribe to `GET /mailboxes/{mailboxId}/events` and call this whenever a frame arrives (a `state.changed` frame's `Email` value is itself a valid `since`). **When the token is too old** (or was minted by a mailbox that has since been rebuilt) you get `410 cannot_calculate_changes`. There is no repair: re-list the mailbox and bootstrap a fresh token. History is kept for 30 days, comfortably longer than the 14-day trash window, so this only happens to a client that has been away a long time.
